suffering, frequently portrayed as unquenchable fire.","primary_basis":["Matthew 5:22, 29–30 associates Gehenna with judgment and warns that the whole person may be cast into it.","Matthew 10:28 and Luke 12:5 describe God as able to destroy or cast a person into Gehenna after death.","Matthew 18:8–9 parallels Gehenna with “eternal fire.”","Matthew 23:15, 33 uses Gehenna as the destination or sentence awaiting the condemned.","Mark 9:43–48 describes Gehenna as unquenchable fire, invoking Isaiah 66:24: “their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.”","Jeremiah 7:31–33 and 19:2–13 supply the Old Testament background: the Valley of Hinnom was associated with child sacrifice, divine judgment, slaughter, and defilement.","2 Kings 23:10 records Josiah’s defilement of Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom because of its association with child sacrifice."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Final annihilation or irreversible destruction: Gehenna represents the complete extinction of the wicked rather than everlasting conscious suffering.","basis":["Matthew 10:28 speaks of God destroying both body and soul in Gehenna.","Images of death, destruction, consuming fire, and discarded corpses are historical or temporal judgment, especially Jerusalem’s destruction in the first century, rather than a postmortem realm.","basis":["Jeremiah 7 and 19 use the Valley of Hinnom as the site and symbol of national catastrophe.","Matthew 23 places Gehenna warnings within Jesus’ denunciation of Jerusalem’s leaders and the approaching judgment upon that generation.","Some interpreters connect the corpse and fire imagery with siege, slaughter, and covenantal judgment."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Finite, corrective, or purgative divine punishment that ultimately serves restoration rather than endless exclusion.","basis":["Fire can function elsewhere in Scripture as purification or testing.","Universalist readings interpret judgment texts alongside passages understood to promise Valley of Hinnom and its associations with idolatry, defilement, corpses, and judgment provide the main referent, without requiring a fully developed doctrine of hell in every occurrence.","basis":["The term is the Greek form of “Valley of Hinnom,” an actual location near Jerusalem.","Jeremiah 7:31–33; 19:2–13 and 2 Kings 23:10 establish its historical associations.","Critical scholarship often distinguishes Jesus’ Gehenna imagery from later, more systematized Christian descriptions of hell."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A burning garbage evil."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad consensus that New Testament Gehenna language evokes divine judgment through the notorious Valley of Hinnom. Traditional eternal hell is the dominant Christian interpretation, but there is no comparable consensus about the precise nature, duration, or mechanism of the punishment. The popular claim that the valley functioned as a perpetually burning municipal garbage dump in Jesus’ day is historically disputed and lacks clear biblical or early contemporary evidence."}
